A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Articulat3D and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–D. Retained and revised content can be reliably matched.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction experiments on three datasets, component ablations, robustness tests, hyperparameter sensitivity, and runtime measurements.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds segmentation-error experiments, real-world joint measurements, and a VideoArtGS-20 comparison in Appendix C.4.

M1.justification: The reported initializer changes substantially. Appendix B.1 replaces v1's assignments based on peak motion energy in sequential time windows with velocity/spatial-feature K-means, revised static detection, and distance-based initialization. Section 3.1 also introduces primitive-based trajectory classification and sparse, near-discrete motion assignments. The subsequent kinematic refinement remains.

E1.justification: v2 retains the three original datasets and adds evaluation on external VideoArtGS-20 sequences and an Articulat3D-Sim scenario with corrupted segmentation masks. Coverage expands within articulated-object reconstruction; novel-view rendering was already covered in v1.

E2.justification: VideoArtGS, previously discussed but not quantitatively evaluated, becomes a comparator on VideoArtGS-20 in Table 6. The RSRD, Articulate Anything, iTACO, and Shape of Motion comparisons in Table 2 remain unchanged.

E3.justification: Appendix C.4 adds joint evaluation against manual annotations for a real-world subset and full-pipeline reruns after inserting contiguous false-positive mask regions. Existing metric definitions, frame-subsampling settings, and baseline configurations remain. Expanded tracking-noise documentation does not establish a changed experiment.

E4.justification: v2 adds segmentation-error sensitivity testing and qualitative novel-view examples in Figure 10. Existing component ablations, tracking-noise robustness, frame-sparsity tests, and learning-rate sensitivity are retained. Table 6's noise-track means reproduce the earlier Table 3 results.

E5.justification: v1 reports point estimates without dispersion. Table 6 introduces mean ± standard deviation across Articulat3D's original dataset results and the added comparisons, substantially expanding statistical reporting. The aggregation unit, seed counts, and repeated-run procedure are unspecified, so this does not establish additional runs.

E6.justification: Tables 2–5 retain their numerical values, but Table 6 substantially extends empirical findings with mask-corruption results, real-world joint errors of 2.02 degrees and 1.61 cm, and external-benchmark comparisons. On VideoArtGS-20, Articulat3D versus VideoArtGS reports PSNR 38.84 versus 37.42, but worse CD-w, 0.15 versus 0.09. Figure 10 adds novel-view renderings.

T1.justification: Appendix B.1 removes mutual-exclusivity and sequential-activation assumptions and replaces temporal-energy assignment mathematics with motion-direction/spatial features, accumulated-motion thresholds, and K-means distances. This substantively changes the initializer's assumptions and definitions. The articulated-kinematics derivations and refinement-loss formulas are retained.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction retain the same central contributions: casual monocular digital-twin reconstruction, two-stage optimization, two introduced benchmarks, and state-of-the-art performance claims. The shortened conclusion preserves their substantive scope.

C2.justification: Appendix C.4 newly explains robustness through inconsistent geometric support for mask errors and subsequent refinement of noisy trajectory initialization. Novel-view results receive a coherent-3D interpretation. The standalone failure discussion, including symmetric-surface and camera–articulation ambiguity caveats, is removed; textureless-surface and independent-joint limitations remain.

D1.justification: v2 documents mask-perturbation shapes and counts and specifies that tracking perturbations preserve visibility, confidence, correspondences, and static labels. It also expands initialization details. Learning rates, hardware, runtimes, and the project link remain unchanged; numerical noise strength and the real-world annotation subset size remain unspecified.

R1.justification: Section 3.1 expands differentiation from Shape of Motion through part-aligned assignments and motion-interval regularization. Appendix C.4 adds positioning against VideoArtGS under its native benchmark protocol. The bibliography retains the same cited works.

P1.justification: Rewriting is concentrated in Section 3.1 and Appendix B.1. v2 adds Appendix C.4 and acknowledgements, removes the standalone failure subsection, shortens the conclusion, and updates affiliations. The overall organization and most existing prose remain.

P2.justification: v2 adds Figure 10 and Table 6 while retaining earlier visual content. The sparsity and dataset figures become Figures 11 and 12. Existing displays are relocated or resized, Figure 8's caption is shortened, and the page canvas and margins change.

improvement.justification: The added direct real-world joint measurements, VideoArtGS comparison, and segmentation-error testing address useful evaluation gaps in v1. Dispersion reporting also improves transparency. These gains are limited by unspecified statistical aggregation and annotation sample sizes, plus an inconsistency introduced in Appendix B.1: Equation 13 uses squared distance while its explanation still describes negative log-probability.
